1408.title: The single life
1408.hook: single people also live a calling of love and service
1408.howItsDone: Single Catholics live the call to holiness in their work, friendships, family and parish, without vows of religious life. The Catechism asks parishes to welcome single people and describes the Church as a home and family for everyone.

segments.voice: Yesterday, marriage as calling: the couple giving the sacrament to each other, and Paul's great sacrament. Your line was holy through each other.

A question single people sometimes get at family weddings: so, when's it your turn? Asked kindly, over cake, as if life were a waiting room and the real thing starts at the altar. Meanwhile, look at one single man's week. Tuesday, he drives his elderly neighbor to the cardiologist. Wednesday, he's the one his sister calls at midnight. Saturday, he coaches nine-year-olds who think he's the funniest man alive. Sunday, he reads at the early Mass. Nobody at the wedding asked about any of that.
screen: `WHEN'S IT YOUR TURN?` → `A WEEK OF ONE SINGLE MAN.` → `NOBODY ASKED ABOUT THAT.`

segments.voice: Start with something easy to skip: the Gospels give Jesus no wife. Neither, as far as his letters let us see, did Paul, and he writes about it to Corinth with real warmth. In the Douay-Rheims: "For I would that all men were even as myself: but every one hath his proper gift from God; one after this manner, and another after that." Notice the word gift. Marriage is a gift; so is the unmarried life. Then he says why it matters: "He that is without a wife, is solicitous for the things that belong to the Lord, how he may please God." The unmarried person, Paul says, has room: for prayer, for friends, for people who need someone to show up. The Catechism speaks to single people directly. It says many live single not by their own choice, because of the circumstances of their lives, and that they are especially close to the heart of Jesus. It asks parishes to open their doors to them, and says no one is without a family in this world: the Church is a home and family for everyone. So the Catholic picture isn't of a person waiting for a vocation to begin. The call to holiness from two days ago is already theirs, whole. Some single people take a vow later, some marry later, and some live single all their lives. None of those seasons is a gap in the calling. Love and service don't need a ring to count. The neighbor at the cardiologist knows that.
screen: `THE GOSPELS GIVE JESUS NO WIFE.` · `EVERY ONE HATH HIS PROPER GIFT.` · `ROOM FOR THE THINGS OF THE LORD.` · `THE CHURCH IS A HOME FOR EVERYONE.` · then, large: `EVERY ONE HATH HIS PROPER GIFT FROM GOD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you know who is single, a friend, an aunt, a widower down the street, or yourself, and one specific way they show up for people: the drive, the call, the meal. If you pray, thank God for them by name, and ask that they be loved as they love. If you don't, let gratitude for them fill the sit.
The single life. In Catholic teaching, a life lived unmarried, by choice or by circumstance, that is already a whole calling to love and service. Today's word.
Your line: a whole calling. No season of life is a waiting room. Same time tomorrow.

1409.title: Religious life
1409.hook: poverty, chastity and obedience, lived in community
1409.howItsDone: Catholic religious sisters, brothers, monks and nuns profess vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, or a formula that contains them, after a time of formation, and live in community under a rule approved by the Church. Some communities profess an additional vow particular to their mission.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the single life: every one hath his proper gift, and room for the things of the Lord. Your line was a whole calling.

A young woman kneels in a chapel before her community: a row of women in the same habit, some old enough to be her grandmother. She holds a card, and her voice shakes a little as she reads from it. She is promising to own nothing of her own, to love no one as a spouse, and to go where she's sent. In some communities, she then lays the card on the altar and signs it there, in front of everyone. Afterward, cake in the convent kitchen and family photos. Her brother still doesn't quite get it. Today's word: evangelical counsels.
screen: `A CARD, READ ALOUD IN A CHAPEL.` → `NOTHING OWNED. NO SPOUSE. SENT.` → `SIGNED ON THE ALTAR.`

segments.voice: Evangelical here doesn't name a church. It means of the Gospel. The counsels are the Gospel's invitations, as opposed to its commands. The Catechism draws the line: the commandments are for everyone; the counsels point to ways of removing whatever, even if not wrong, gets in the way of love. It names them: poverty, chastity and obedience. Take poverty. A rich young man asks Jesus what he still lacks. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus answers: "If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come follow me." He goes away sad, Matthew says, because he had a great deal. The counsel is the part he couldn't do. Chastity, for a religious, means celibacy: leaving marriage aside so the heart is free for God and for everyone. Obedience means putting your will into the hands of the community and its superior, as Jesus put his into the Father's. The Catechism says it's professing these counsels, in a stable state of life the Church recognizes, that marks consecrated life. And it's lived together: a shared table, a rule, a chapel, and a superior who sends them. Not every community words the vows the same way. Benedict's Rule has a monk promise stability, faithfulness to the monastic way of life, and obedience, and Catholics read the same counsels inside it. Some orders add a vow of their own. The three run underneath.

If you pray, ask God to keep them faithful and glad in their vows, and to send the people their communities need. If you don't, hold them with thanks for one thing they gave away.
Evangelical counsels. The Gospel's invitations to poverty, chastity and obedience, which religious sisters and brothers profess as vows and live in community. Today's word.
Your line: three vows. Each one clears away something that gets in the way of love. Rest well.

1410.title: Deacons
1410.hook: since 1967 permanent deacons, often married, serve in the Latin Church
1410.howItsDone: Catholic deacons are ordained by a bishop. At Mass they proclaim the Gospel, may preach, and assist at the altar; they also baptize, witness marriages, lead funeral rites and serve in works of charity. In the Latin Church, permanent deacons may be married men who keep their jobs and families.

segments.voice: Yesterday, religious life: the evangelical counsels, and a rich young man who went away sad. Your line was three vows.

Sunday morning. A man in an alb steps up to the ambo to proclaim the Gospel. His stole doesn't hang straight down like the priest's: it crosses his chest from one shoulder to the opposite hip, like a sash. He reads, then preaches, and somewhere in the homily mentions his grandson's soccer game. In the third pew, his wife rolls her eyes and smiles. On Monday he's back at his job; on Thursday evening, at the county jail, leading a Bible study. He is ordained, and married, and neither a priest nor on his way to becoming one. Today, deacons.
screen: `A STOLE WORN LIKE A SASH.` → `HIS WIFE IN THE THIRD PEW.` → `ORDAINED, BUT NOT A PRIEST.`

segments.voice: A deacon is a servant. The Catechism calls Christ himself the deacon, or servant, of all. In Mark's Gospel, Jesus says it of himself, in the Douay-Rheims: "For the Son of man also is not come to be ministered unto: but to minister, and to give his life a redemption for many." To minister there means to serve, to wait on. Back on day five hundred forty-one, you met the seven in Acts: Greek-speaking widows overlooked in the daily food, and seven men full of the Spirit and wisdom, chosen by the community, with the apostles laying hands on them. Stephen was one. Tradition sees in them the first deacons. By the time Paul writes to Philippi, he greets the church "with the bishops and deacons." What does a deacon do? The Catechism lists it: assisting the bishop and priests at the Eucharist, giving communion, witnessing and blessing marriages, proclaiming the Gospel and preaching, presiding at funerals, and giving himself to works of charity. He does not consecrate the Eucharist or hear confessions. He is ordained, the Catechism says, not for priesthood but for service. And there are two kinds. Men on the road to priesthood are ordained deacons first. But the Second Vatican Council asked that the diaconate be restored in the Latin Church as a permanent rank, open to men of mature age, including married men. So the deacon at the ambo is something old and something renewed at once: a married man, ordained to serve.
screen: `CHRIST, THE SERVANT OF ALL.` · `SEVEN CHOSEN TO SERVE THE WIDOWS.` · `GOSPEL, ALTAR, CHARITY.` · `RESTORED AS A PERMANENT RANK.` · then, large: `NOT TO BE MINISTERED UNTO, BUT TO MINISTER.`

1411.title: Hermits and consecrated virgins
1411.howItsDone: Diocesan hermits profess the evangelical counsels publicly before their bishop and live in solitude, silence and prayer under his guidance. Consecrated virgins are consecrated by their bishop in a solemn rite and may live in community or in the world, some keeping their ordinary jobs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, deacons: servants, like the seven chosen to feed the widows. Your line was servants.

A hospital pharmacist finishes her shift, takes the bus home to a small apartment, and prays the Church's evening prayer at her kitchen table. On her right hand is a plain ring. Years ago, in her cathedral, the bishop consecrated her to Christ, and she went back to work the next morning. A few hours' drive away, a man lives alone in a cabin on land his diocese lent him. He has made vows into the hands of his bishop. He grows vegetables, keeps silence, and prays through the night for a world that mostly doesn't know he's there. Neither belongs to an order. Both callings reach back to the early Church.
screen: `A PHARMACIST WITH A PLAIN RING.` → `A CABIN, A VOW, A SILENCE.` → `NEITHER BELONGS TO AN ORDER.`

segments.voice: Back on day two hundred eighty-two, a monk moved into a small house in the woods. The prophet Elijah, worn out and running for his life, goes into the desert and on to the mountain of God, and the Lord isn't in the wind, or the earthquake, or the fire. In the Douay-Rheims: "and after the fire a whistling of a gentle air." Hermits go looking for that whisper. In the early centuries, tradition says, men and women went into the Egyptian desert to pray alone; the Life of Antony tells of one. The Catechism describes hermits today: giving their lives to the praise of God and the salvation of the world through a stricter separation from the world, the silence of solitude, and constant prayer and penance. Church law recognizes a hermit who professes the evangelical counsels publicly in the hands of the diocesan bishop and lives under his guidance. Now the consecrated virgin. The Catechism says that from apostolic times, Christian virgins, called by the Lord, gave themselves to him with an undivided heart. The Church keeps a rite for it today: a woman who has never married is consecrated by her bishop in a solemn liturgy, joined to Christ as a bride. She may live in a community, or in the world, at her own job, in her own apartment, under the bishop's care. The Catechism calls the hermit's life a reminder of the inward side of the Church's mystery: what is quietly happening with God underneath.
screen: `ELIJAH IN THE DESERT.` · `A WHISTLING OF A GENTLE AIR.` · `VOWS INTO THE BISHOP'S HANDS.` · `A VIRGIN CONSECRATED IN THE WORLD.` · then, large: `AFTER THE FIRE, A WHISTLING OF A GENTLE AIR.`

segments.voice: Somewhere today a hermit is keeping silence, and a woman with a plain ring is at work, and nobody around them knows. Let this quiet be a small share in theirs. If you pray, ask God to strengthen people whose callings no one sees; if you don't, hold them in mind, unnamed, with good will.
Hermits and consecrated virgins. Callings from the Church's early centuries, still lived today: solitude and prayer under a bishop, and lifelong consecration to Christ. Today's word.
Your line: ancient callings. Still lived today, mostly where no one is looking. I'll be here tomorrow.

1412.title: Secular institutes
1412.hook: consecrated people living ordinary jobs in the world
1412.howItsDone: Members of secular institutes make a commitment to poverty, chastity and obedience while keeping ordinary jobs and homes. They usually wear no habit, and some institutes ask members to keep their consecration private.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hermits and consecrated virgins: a cabin and a vow, a plain ring from a bishop. Your line was ancient callings.

The security guard on the night shift. The accountant two desks over. The woman who runs the hardware store and remembers which screws you bought last time. Any of them could have made vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, and you would never know. No habit, no convent, no title on the name badge. They pay rent, file taxes, go to the office party, and live a consecration the Church recognizes. Today, a calling designed to be hard to spot.
screen: `THE GUARD, THE ACCOUNTANT, THE SHOPKEEPER.` → `NO HABIT, NO CONVENT.` → `A CALLING HARD TO SPOT.`

segments.voice: First, the name. A secular institute is a form of consecrated life, but secular here doesn't mean unbelieving. It means in the world, in ordinary time and ordinary places. The Code of Canon Law describes these institutes as groups whose members, living in the world, strive for the perfection of charity and work to make the world holy, especially from within. From within is the key phrase. Members commit to the evangelical counsels, poverty, chastity and obedience, by the bonds each institute sets, but they live in the ordinary conditions of the world: alone, with their families, or in small groups. Some institutes are for laypeople, some for priests. A lay member stays a layperson; a priest member stays a diocesan priest. Then the picture. Jesus told a parable about bread. In the Douay-Rheims: "The kingdom of heaven is like to leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal, until the whole was leavened." Notice the word hid. Yeast doesn't sit on top of the dough looking holy. It disappears into it, and the whole loaf changes. The Code uses the same picture: these members act like leaven. Last, the quiet. Some institutes ask members to keep their consecration private, so they can work anywhere, as colleagues rather than visitors. Their witness is the work itself: a fair invoice, an unhurried hour with a difficult patient, a meeting run honestly. Yesterday's hermits went out to the edges. These people stay in the middle of everything, and the point is that nobody notices.
screen: `SECULAR MEANS IN THE WORLD.` · `VOWS, LIVED AT HOME AND AT WORK.` · `LIKE LEAVEN HIDDEN IN THE DOUGH.` · `THE WITNESS IS THE WORK ITSELF.` · then, large: `UNTIL THE WHOLE WAS LEAVENED.`

segments.voice: You may not know anyone who has made these vows, and that's the point. Let your mind walk through the places you pass in a week, a clinic, a classroom, an office, a shop, where someone may be living a hidden promise. If you pray, ask God to strengthen them, whoever they are; if you don't, wish them well, and let the faces you pass feel a little less ordinary.
Secular institutes. Consecrated life lived in the world, from within, like yeast in the dough. Today's word.

1413.title: The parish
1413.hook: the local family of the Church
1413.howItsDone: Catholics normally belong to the parish where they live, and register there for the sacraments and parish life. Personal parishes also serve people of a particular rite, language or nationality.

segments.voice: Yesterday, secular institutes: vows lived in ordinary jobs, like leaven in the dough. Your line was hidden in the world.

The boxes are still taped shut. Here's a small surprise for anyone who has moved: when a Catholic settles at a new address, Church law gives them a new parish along with it, before any registration form is filled in. As a general rule, the law draws parishes by territory, so the street you sleep on decides which parish is yours. The church down the road may have a bingo night, a youth group with a broken ping-pong table, and a priest who still hasn't learned your name. It's yours anyway.
screen: `THE BOXES ARE STILL TAPED SHUT.` → `THE STREET DECIDES THE PARISH.` → `IT'S YOURS ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Back on day ninety-seven, you walked through a parish door. Today, what a parish is. The word often means the building, the brick church with the parking lot. The Code of Canon Law describes something else: a community of the Christian faithful, set up for good, within a particular church, whose pastoral care is entrusted to a pastor under the bishop's authority. A community first; the building is where it gathers. How do you belong? As a general rule, the Code says, a parish is territorial: it takes in all the faithful who live within its borders. There are also personal parishes, formed around a rite, a language or a nationality, so a Spanish-speaking or Vietnamese-speaking community may have a parish that crosses the map. But the default is simple: you belong where you live. What happens there? The Book of Acts describes the first believers in Jerusalem, in the Douay-Rheims: "And they were persevering in the doctrine of the apostles, and in the communication of the breaking of bread, and in prayers." Teaching, the breaking of bread, prayer. A parish is where those happen within reach of your front door: baptisms and funerals, confessions on Saturday, the Sunday Mass, a food pantry in the basement. And why it matters on a Tuesday: a parish isn't chosen for its music or its preacher, though some people do shop around. It's given, like a family. That means sharing a pew with people you didn't pick, and that is part of what makes it a family.

1414.title: The diocese
1414.hook: a local church gathered around its bishop
1414.howItsDone: A Catholic parish belongs to a diocese, or a similar local church, led by a bishop, whose chair stands in the cathedral. Catholics pray for their bishop by name in the Eucharistic Prayer at Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the parish: a community before a building, drawn by where you live. Your line was home base.

Inside a cathedral, somewhere near the altar, stands a chair. Sometimes it's carved stone, sometimes plain wood with a high back. Tourists walk past it on the way to the stained glass. It waits for one person, the bishop, and it's what makes that church a cathedral rather than just a large parish. Around that chair, a whole region of parishes is gathered: city churches, country chapels, schools, hospitals. Today, the diocese.
screen: `A CHAIR NEAR THE ALTAR.` → `IT WAITS FOR THE BISHOP.` → `A WHOLE REGION AROUND IT.`

segments.voice: What is a diocese? The Code of Canon Law describes it as a portion of the people of God entrusted to a bishop, to be shepherded with the help of his priests. Portion of the people is the phrase: like the parish, a diocese is people before it's a map. The Second Vatican Council went further. In a diocese, it taught, the one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church of Christ is truly present and at work. That's a strong claim. A diocese isn't a branch office of a company headquartered somewhere else. It's the whole Church, present in one place, gathered around its bishop. The idea is old. Ignatius of Antioch, writing to Christians in Smyrna on the journey that, tradition says, ended in his martyrdom, put it this way: "Wheresoever the bishop shall appear, there let the people be; even as where Jesus may be, there is the universal Church." The chair in the cathedral is a sign of that: teaching and shepherding, rooted in one place. Now look back at the week: the single life, a whole calling; religious life and its three vows; deacons, the servants; hermits and consecrated virgins; secular institutes, hidden in the world; and the parish, home base. Every one of those callings is lived somewhere, and that somewhere is a local church. The diocese is where all of them belong together, under one bishop, around one altar.
